title: Anne Frank’s diary reaches the world, 1947
description: Anne Frank wrote her diary while hiding in the annex behind this canal house until her arrest in 1944. Her cousin recalls the family and how the diary came to be published in 1947.

title: Medieval Amsterdam: the 1345 miracle and the Reformation
description: Amsterdam first drew crowds as a pilgrimage town after a reported miracle in 1345, then broke with Catholic rule in 1578. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook walk through its early centuries.

title: Amsterdam’s canals and the Dutch Golden Age
description: The canal ring was dug in the 1600s to house the merchants who made Amsterdam rich. Part two of the walking tour covers the canals, the Golden Age and the city’s later liberal reputation.

title: The world’s first same-sex weddings, Amsterdam 2001
description: At midnight on 1 April 2001, four couples married in Amsterdam as the Netherlands became the first country to allow same-sex marriage. One couple recalls the night.

title: How Athenian democracy worked
description: The citizens’ assembly of ancient Athens met on this hill to debate and vote. Cambridge historian Paul Cartledge explains how the system started and who could take part.

title: The Athens famine under German occupation, 1941–42
description: After Germany occupied Greece in 1941, food ran out in Athens and tens of thousands died that winter. A woman who lived through it and historian Mark Mazower describe what happened.

title: Athens revives the Olympics, 1896
description: The first modern Olympic Games opened in 1896 in this rebuilt marble stadium. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook start there and follow the Games up to the Second World War.

title: The storming of parliament and Milošević’s fall, 2000
description: On 5 October 2000, crowds protesting a stolen election stormed the federal parliament, and Milošević stood down hours later. Otpor student leader Srđa Popović recalls the day.

channel: Stuff You Missed in History Class
title: Kristallnacht, November 1938
description: On 9–10 November 1938, Nazis attacked Jewish homes, shops and synagogues across Germany. The episode covers how the violence was organised and what followed for German Jews.

title: Inside Hitler’s bunker, from 1945 to its demolition
description: Hitler spent his last weeks in a bunker under the Reich Chancellery garden and killed himself there in April 1945. Photographs show the rooms as they were found and what became of them.

title: Fighting for Berlin, April–May 1945
description: In the last weeks of the war the Red Army fought its way into Berlin street by street. A Soviet woman soldier and a German schoolboy who fought on opposite sides describe the battle.

title: Frederick the Great of Prussia
description: Frederick II ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786, made it a military power and built Sanssouci as his retreat. Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss his wars, his writing and his court.

title: Queer life in Weimar Berlin
description: In the 1920s the streets around Nollendorfplatz were the centre of Berlin’s gay and lesbian bars and clubs. Greg Jenner and guests look at queer life in the Weimar Republic and how the Nazis ended it.

title: The Battle of Waterloo, 1815
description: On 18 June 1815, Wellington and Blücher defeated Napoleon south of Brussels and ended his rule for good. Dan Snow and his father Peter Snow go through the battle.

title: Miners sent against protesters in Bucharest, 1990
description: In June 1990 the government brought coal miners into Bucharest to break up the protest camp in University Square, beating students and opponents. A Romanian public radio history feature.

title: The Legionnaire uprising and pogrom, January 1941
description: In January 1941 the fascist Iron Guard rose against Antonescu and, over three days, killed scores of Jews in Bucharest and wrecked synagogues and shops. A Romanian public radio history feature.

title: Raoul Wallenberg, Budapest’s vanished rescuer
description: Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved thousands of Budapest Jews in 1944 with protective passes. He went to meet Soviet officers in January 1945 and was never seen in public again.

channel: Stuff You Missed in History Class
title: Struensee, the Royal Doctor Who Ran Denmark
description: In 1772 Struensee, the mentally ill Christian VII’s doctor, de facto ruler and the queen’s lover, was arrested after a masked ball at this court theatre. The episode tells how he rose and fell.

title: Denmark–Norway and the Atlantic Slave Trade
description: Sugar, rum and the profits of slavery in the Danish West Indies were stored in this harbourside warehouse. The episode covers how Denmark–Norway ran forts in Ghana, shipped enslaved Africans and held Caribbean colonies.

title: The Great Irish Famine, 1845–52
description: These gaunt bronze figures face the quay where emigrant ships left during the famine. Historians explain why the potato blight killed a million people and drove two million more out of Ireland.

title: Jonathan Swift’s ‘A Modest Proposal’
description: Swift was Dean of St Patrick’s for over 30 years and is buried in the nave. In 1729 he wrote this satire suggesting the Irish poor sell their children as food. The episode looks at the pamphlet and its targets.

title: The Covenanters and the National Covenant, 1638
description: In 1638 Scots signed the National Covenant here, rejecting Charles I’s changes to their church. Historians trace the covenants from James VI to the killings of the 1680s.

title: The Union of Scotland and England, 1707
description: Scotland’s parliament met in this hall until it voted itself out of existence in 1707. A Scottish historian explains what each country wanted from the union and why it went through.

title: The Black Death in Boccaccio’s Florence
description: Boccaccio’s Decameron opens in this church in 1348, as ten young Florentines meet and agree to escape the plague. The episode uses the book to show how people in the city lived through the Black Death.

title: The Soviet Invasion of Finland, 1939–40
description: The Winter War began on 30 November 1939 with Soviet bombs falling on Helsinki. The video covers the invasion and Finland’s 105-day defence. The national Winter War memorial stands on this square.

title: The Gezi Park Protests, 2013
description: A 2013 sit-in to save this park’s trees grew into protests across Turkey. The actor and activist Memet Ali Alabora tells how one social media post changed his life.

title: The Lisbon Regicide, 1908
description: On 1 February 1908 gunmen shot King Carlos I and his heir in an open carriage as it turned out of this square. The episode explains the killing and how it led to the end of Portugal’s monarchy in 1910.

title: A thousand years at the Tower of London
description: William the Conqueror’s fortress has been palace, prison, armoury and execution site. Dan Snow walks through its sieges, escapes, beheadings and famous prisoners, from Anne Boleyn onward.

title: The Tower as a medieval prison, from Flambard to the Princes
description: Recorded inside the Tower after hours. Two medievalists tell the escape stories of Ranulf Flambard and Roger Mortimer and discuss its best-known prisoners, including the two princes who vanished in 1483.

title: The history of Westminster Abbey
description: Every English monarch since 1066 has been crowned here. The film follows the abbey from Edward the Confessor’s church through Henry III’s Gothic rebuild to its coronations and royal tombs.

title: The Gunpowder Plot, 1605
description: On 5 November 1605 Guy Fawkes was found with nearly a ton of gunpowder in an undercroft beneath the House of Lords. The episode covers the Catholic plotters, their aims and how the plan was exposed.

title: The execution of Charles I, 1649
description: On 30 January 1649 Charles I stepped out of a window here onto a scaffold and was beheaded in front of a large crowd. The episode explains how it came to that and what it meant for Britain.

title: London and the Great Plague of 1665
place: Site of the Bedlam burial ground, Liverpool Street
description: Plague killed around a fifth of Londoners in 1665. Historian Vanessa Harding describes how it spread, how the city responded and how ordinary people tried to cope.

title: St Paul’s and the Second Great Fire of London, 1940
description: On 29 December 1940 German bombs set the City ablaze around St Paul’s. Dan Snow tours the bomb damage with a guide and hears the story behind the famous photo of the dome rising above the smoke.

title: Christopher Wren, the architect of St Paul’s
description: Wren was an astronomer and anatomist before he rebuilt London after the 1666 fire. Historian Steven Brindle traces his life and how he came to design the cathedral.

title: Inside Churchill’s underground War Rooms
place: Churchill War Rooms, King Charles Street
description: Beneath Whitehall, Churchill’s government ran the war from a reinforced basement during the Blitz. The film goes through the map room, cabinet room and the rooms where staff lived and slept.

title: The Peasants’ Revolt and the death of Wat Tyler, 1381
description: In June 1381 rebels from Essex and Kent took London, stormed the Tower and met the boy king Richard II at Smithfield, where Wat Tyler was killed. With medievalist Eleanor Janega.

title: The Atocha lawyers massacre, 1977
description: In January 1977, as Spain moved toward democracy, far-right gunmen burst into a labour law office here and shot dead five people. The killings and the huge silent funeral march that followed are covered.

title: The Beer Hall Putsch ends in gunfire at the Feldherrnhalle, 1923
description: On 9 November 1923 Hitler’s marchers were stopped by Bavarian police in front of this loggia; the shooting killed 4 police and 16 Nazis. Mark Felton goes through the failed coup.

title: The liberation of Dachau, 1945
description: The first Nazi concentration camp opened at Dachau in 1933. On 29 April 1945 American troops reached it; Mark Felton covers the camp and the day it was liberated.

title: The 22 July attacks, 2011
description: On 22 July 2011 a far-right extremist set off a bomb at the government offices here, then shot dozens of young people at a summer camp on Utøya. A survivor tells her story.

title: Westminster Abbey, coronation church since 1066
description: Monarchs have been crowned here since William the Conqueror on Christmas Day 1066. Historian David Carpenter, who grew up in the abbey, answers listener questions about its long history.

title: The St Bartholomew’s Day Massacre, 1572
description: Days after a royal wedding meant to reconcile Catholics and Protestants, Catholic mobs killed thousands of Huguenots across Paris. Historians explain who ordered it and why the killing spread.

title: The Dreyfus Affair and the officer stripped of his rank
description: In 1895 Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer wrongly convicted of spying for Germany, was publicly degraded in this courtyard. Oxford historian Ruth Harris explains how the case split France for a decade.

channel: Stuff You Missed in History Class
title: How Paris moved six million dead into old quarries
place: Catacombs of Paris entrance, Place Denfert-Rochereau
description: In the 18th century Paris had collapsing limestone mines underfoot and overflowing cemeteries. The hosts explain how the city solved both by moving the bones of some six million people into the tunnels.

title: Jan Hus and the Hussite Wars
description: Jan Hus preached church reform here in Czech until he was burned as a heretic in 1415. Eleanor Janega and Matt Lewis trace how his death set off decades of revolt and crusades against Bohemia.

title: The assassination of Reinhard Heydrich, 1942
place: Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Resslova
description: Czechoslovak parachutists ambushed the Nazi governor Reinhard Heydrich in 1942, then made their last stand in this church crypt. The episode tells the story of the operation and its aftermath.

channel: Stuff You Missed in History Class
title: Jón Arason, Iceland’s last Catholic bishop
description: Bishop Jón Arason led resistance to the Lutheran Reformation imposed by the Danish crown, and was beheaded at Skálholt in 1550 with two of his sons. The hosts tell his story and how Iceland turned Lutheran.

title: The 1949 riot over Iceland joining NATO
description: In March 1949 crowds outside parliament threw stones as MPs voted to join NATO, and police answered with tear gas. The episode tells the story of the riot and why the vote divided Icelanders.

title: Garibaldi and the unification of Italy
description: Garibaldi fought French troops on this hill in 1849 to defend the short-lived Roman Republic. Historians trace his life and the long campaign to unite Italy, which ended with Rome taken in 1870.

title: The fall of Mussolini, 1943
description: Mussolini ruled from this palace and gave speeches from its balcony. In July 1943 his own Fascist Grand Council voted against him here. The episode explains how his power collapsed and how he died.

title: Filming The Third Man in occupied Vienna
description: In 1948 Carol Reed filmed a thriller in a bombed-out Vienna split between four Allied powers. This short episode recalls the shoot, Orson Welles’ Harry Lime and the city the film captured.

title: The trial and execution of Louis XVI, 1793
description: Louis XVI was guillotined on this square in January 1793 after a trial by the National Convention. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook cover the trial, the vote and the execution.

title: The student revolt of May 1968
description: In May 1968 students occupied the Sorbonne and fought police behind barricades in the Latin Quarter, and a general strike followed. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook tell how the unrest brought France to a halt.

title: The Wannsee Conference, 1942
place: House of the Wannsee Conference, Am Großen Wannsee 56–58
description: In January 1942 senior Nazi officials met in this lakeside villa to organise the murder of Europe’s Jews. The episode marks 70 years since the meeting and what was decided there.

title: Surviving Ireland’s Magdalene laundries
place: Former Magdalene laundry, Seán McDermott Street
description: Catholic orders ran laundries where women and girls worked unpaid behind locked doors; Dublin’s last closed here in 1996. A woman sent to one as a young girl describes her time inside.

title: Life in the Kraków ghetto, 1941
description: In March 1941 the Nazis forced Kraków’s Jews across the river into a walled ghetto in Podgórze, cleared in 1943 from this square. The episode recalls the move and life inside.

title: Rome’s Jews, the gold ransom and the 1943 raid
place: Largo 16 Ottobre 1943, Via del Portico d’Ottavia
description: In September 1943 the SS demanded 50 kg of gold from Rome’s Jews in return for their safety. Weeks later, on 16 October, over 1,000 were seized in the ghetto and deported to Auschwitz.

title: The kidnap and murder of Aldo Moro, 1978
description: The Red Brigades kidnapped former prime minister Aldo Moro in March 1978 and held him for 55 days. His body was left in a car on this street, between the Christian Democrat and Communist party offices.
